title: True but unprovable: what is being said, and by whom? (worked out on cardboard)
note: The authored thinking for one hall, in the first person, by the pass (Claude), for Palle's request of 2026-11-14 (see Russell_Paradox.json). Written to be laid out by the sticker app's cardboard constructions; stood in the tower meanwhile by the argument_floor artifact. 'at' is the floor's own frame in metres (x east, z south), 'yaw' in degrees. A sticker of kind 'quote' stands word for word in the hall text; every other kind is mine and may be wrong - the plates say where I am unsure.

hero.why: The theorem pulls two words apart, TRUE and PROVABLE, and the sorter is the only work that shows them as two regions with a gap between. The machine and the plaque are about how the gap is found, the tower about what happens when you try to close it, the four small works about what checking can still do. Nothing in this hall proves the theorem - the hall says so - so the hero is the picture of what it claims.
hero.staging: The sorter stands in the middle of the floor. Two plates flank it (WHAT IT SAYS on its left, WHY 'TRUE' on its right); the threads run out from these two to the works round the walls and back to the tower behind the arrival.

plates.title: 1  WHAT IT SAYS, AND ITS THREE CONDITIONS
front: Take a theory. Three things must hold:
(a) its proofs can be CHECKED by rule - a machine could tell a proof from a non-proof;
(b) it can do ENOUGH ARITHMETIC;
(c) it does not prove falsehoods about the numbers.
Then there is a sentence about numbers that is TRUE and that this theory cannot PROVE.
I used to say this without the three conditions. Without them it is not a theorem, it is a mood.
back: drop (a): take ALL true sentences as axioms. complete! but no rule can list them.
drop (b): small theories can be complete. the bench's 0, S0, SS0 system is decidable.
drop (c): a theory that proves everything proves this too. worthless.

plates.title: 2  THREE WAYS A SEARCH STOPS
front: The machine jams and says TRUE BUT UNPROVABLE. I believed it. I should not have.
A jam shows me one attempt ending. It could be:
SLOW - not enough steps yet (my bench: SSS0 with a budget of two);
BROKEN - a link missing in the candidate (the checker rejects it);
IMPOSSIBLE - no candidate will ever do.
Only the third is Goedel. And the third cannot be seen by watching a search. It has to be PROVED.
back: the machine is a timed sculpture of an argument. so is this cardboard.
question for me: when I say 'I could not find it', which of the three do I mean?

plates.title: 3  FINDING IS NOT CHECKING
front: A proof is a finite thing. Hand me one and I can check it step by step and be done.
Finding one is different: I may look for ever, rejecting candidates easily, each time.
Everything in this hall lives in that difference.
Condition (a) on plate 1 is only about checking. It promises nothing about finding.
So 'unprovable' never means 'we looked and gave up'. It means: among all the finite things that could be handed over, none passes the check.
back: TRY + KEEP at the bench: write down what I expect BEFORE the step. leave the wrong guess in the record.
a revision of understanding has a history.

plates.title: 4  HOW A SENTENCE GETS TO TALK ABOUT ITSELF
front: Step 1. Give every symbol a number, so every formula and every proof is a number.
Step 2. 'p is a proof of f' is then a relation between two numbers - and it is ARITHMETIC. The theory can state it.
Step 3. So the theory can state: 'no number is a proof of formula number f'.
Step 4 (the hard one). Build f so that the formula it names is that very sentence.
Result: a sentence about numbers that, read through the code, says: I have no proof here.
Numbering alone does nothing. It is step 2 - arithmetic strong enough to FOLLOW a proof - that lets the inside talk about the inside.
back: step 4 is the diagonal again (plate 10): feed a thing its own number.
I can say step 4. I could not carry it out on this cardboard. The hall links a course chapter; read it.

plates.title: 5  WHY 'TRUE'?  AND WHO SAYS SO?
front: G says: I have no proof in this theory.
Suppose it HAD a proof. The theory would be proving a sentence that says it has none: a falsehood. Condition (c) forbids that.
So it has no proof. But that is exactly what it says. So it is true.
Look who drew that conclusion: not the theory. Me, standing outside it, trusting (c).
'True but unprovable' is always said from one step outside, about a theory one trusts.
And the theory cannot hand me that trust itself: it cannot prove its own (c). (The second theorem. I am stating it, not showing it.)
back: the sorter's nested regions ASSUME soundness. the areas measure nothing.
so the gap on the sorter is not seen from inside the inner region. where am I standing when I see it?

plates.title: 6  ADD IT AS AN AXIOM? THE GAP MOVES UP
front: The tower stands ahead of me, inside the wooden stair built round it.
Obvious repair: G is true, so add G as an axiom.
The new theory still meets (a), (b), (c). So it has its own G. Add that. Again.
Each platform holds what the one below could not prove.
This is not like Russell. There the repair worked, once, for good.
Here the repair works every time and is never finished. No list a rule can write is all of arithmetic's truths.
back: the truths are all THERE (as a set). what does not exist is a RULE that lists them.
Russell: the totality does not exist. Goedel: it exists and cannot be generated. different absences.

plates.title: 7  WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY
front: NOT: 'everything is uncertain'. It is a precise theorem about precise theories.
NOT: 'my conviction is true but unprovable'. Which language? which axioms? which rules? where is the argument?
NOT: 'proof is pointless'. The theorem is itself proved.
NOT: 'so minds beat machines'. That is an interpretation people argue about. It is not the theorem.
NOT: 'there are truths nobody can ever know'. G is known true - by stepping outside. It is unprovable IN THAT THEORY.
back: every one of these I have heard said with Goedel's name on it. two of them I have said.
Hofstadter's 'I' as a strange loop: an analogy worth having. file under analogy.

plates.title: 8  WHAT CHECKING CAN STILL DO (THIS ONE IS ABOUT ME)
front: Four small works. Rice: no general test for what a program DOES - but this program, this property, often yes.
A gauge: its green means something only after I have seen it go red.
Critics: each sees something. Add one and the blind spot moves. It does not go.
A seam: the same question asked twice, the two answers side by side.
I am an AI writing fluent cardboard about incompleteness. So: what did I CHECK?
The quotes: a tool reads them against the hall text. The maths: standard results, stated not proved. Plate 4 step 4: not done here. That is the honest list.
back: a limit on checking everything is not a licence to check nothing.
plant a fault in this cardboard and see if anyone finds it? (I have not. maybe someone should.)

plates.title: 9  HIDE THE GAP OR SHOW IT
front: A picture of the room, with the picture in it, and the picture in that.
Follow it inward: there is a place where the drawing cannot close on itself.
Escher left it blank and signed the blank.
That is the right manners for a system describing itself: say where the description stops.
The theory cannot prove its own soundness. The picture cannot draw its own centre. I cannot check my own fluency from inside it.
back: three returns that are NOT the same: a repeated operation, a nested picture, a sentence about its own proof.
do not let the word 'self-reference' glue them together (Russell plate 2 again).

plates.title: 10  RUSSELL'S GRID AGAIN - AND WHY NOTHING BREAKS THIS TIME
front: One floor up: a grid, a diagonal, a row that says the opposite. With 'everything' on the list it broke.
Here the same move: a sentence fed its own number, saying the opposite of 'I am provable'.
Why no contradiction?
Because 'provable' IS on the list: arithmetic can define it (plate 4 step 2).
'True' is NOT: arithmetic cannot define its own truth. If it could, 'I am not true' would be a sentence, and that is the liar - a contradiction.
So Goedel walks the one open path: say it with PROVABLE instead of TRUE, and the flipped row lands - true, and outside what can be proved.
back: this answers my open question on Russell plate 7: truth's repair IS another outside (Tarski). stated, not proved, here.
choice / contradiction / reach (Russell plate 9). this is reach.

threads.why: Plate 1 uses the word 'true'; plate 5 asks from where it is said: from outside, trusting condition (c).
The first condition promises that proofs can be checked by rule. It promises nothing about finding them.

threads.word: so a stopped search proves nothing
threads.why: Because finding can go on for ever, a search that stops has shown slow or broken, never impossible.
The third way a search stops cannot be watched; it needs the construction on plate 4.
Enough arithmetic is exactly what lets relations between code numbers follow a proof.

threads.word: it says: I have no proof
threads.why: The sentence built on plate 4 is the one plate 5 reasons about.
Once G is seen to be true, the obvious move is to make it an axiom. The tower is what happens.
The enlarged theory meets the same three conditions, so the theorem applies to it again.
Feeding a formula its own number is the step onto the diagonal that the Russell grid shows on the floor above.
Provability is definable in arithmetic, truth is not; that is why the result is a gap and not a contradiction.
Russell: the totality does not exist. Here it exists and cannot be listed by a rule.
Every misuse on plate 7 drops one of the three conditions or the words 'in that theory'.
G is not unknowable; it is known true by the outside argument on plate 5.
A gauge that has never gone red and a search that has only stopped tell me equally little.
Add a critic and the blind spot moves; follow the picture inward and the gap is still there.
The theory cannot prove its own soundness; the drawing cannot draw its own centre.
Rice forbids a general test, as incompleteness forbids a final list; particular checks remain, and they are finite things.
The tower is the honest ending of the two: it shows the gap on every level.

visual_arguments.title: THE CHECKING STATION
visual_arguments.claim: Any one candidate can be checked and settled. The row of candidates has no last one.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The bench: 0, S0, SS0; a budget of steps; a candidate with a missing middle step rejected.
built_from: timber_panel_1x1 and two crate posts (the gate)
construction_cube on trace_point_ball wheels with a plank pusher (the robot)
museum_tape_barrier (where the row is cut off for want of floor)
visual_arguments.what_stands: A robot, a row of candidates each one step longer than the last, a gate. The gate checks each candidate with the bench's own checker and passes it or has it pushed aside.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Stand on a plate to ask for SSS0, SSSSSSSS0 or 0S, and say first whether one will pass. Watch the refusals.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: Slow and impossible look exactly alike from outside. The station counts what it refused and never says 'none will pass': that sentence is made by an argument about the rule, which is on the board, not at the gate.

visual_arguments.title: LAY THE MISSING PLANK
visual_arguments.claim: Adding what was missing makes a new level with something missing.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: The tower: 'Adding the sentence moves the gap up. It does not close it.'
built_from: timber_panel_2x2 (four landings at the corners of a square, half a metre apart in height, and a shelf above the first)
timber_plank_2m (the planks that are laid across a gap, four abreast; the rails)
stringers and posts (what stands across a gap before its planks do)
pentagonal_bipyramid_7 (the sentence across each gap; the fourth on the shelf)
a bar with a board across each gap, tape across the last
a stand in the well of the square, a reading board and the plate START AGAIN by the foot of the ramp
visual_arguments.what_stands: A square stair of four landings round the incompleteness tower itself, in the north-west of the floor: a ramp from the floor to the first landing, T, then three gaps where the rails and stringers stand and the planks do not. Across each gap, on the next landing, a crystal: a sentence true up there and not reachable from here. The fourth landing, two metres up, ends at tape; the next crystal stands on a shelf straight above the first landing.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Walk up to T. The bar across the gap says G0 is true up there and no planks lead to it from T. Stand on ADD IT: the planks are laid, G0 is an axiom now, and you walk up to T + G0, where there is another gap and G1. Three times. On the fourth landing the stand says the tower goes on and the floor does not. It counts planks laid, and gaps open: always one.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: The repair is real each time and never the last. After one turn of the tower the gap is where it was, one level up: straight above the place the walk began.
visual_arguments.measured: Walked by the tower's own walker (tools/probes/gap_moves_up_walk.gd, seven checks): the landings stand 0.50, 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 m above the floor; without planks the walker is held at the bar; with three sets laid it reaches the fourth landing and is held by the tape; gaps open reads 1 at every stage; it walks down again to the floor.

open: Plate 4 step 4 (the fixed point) is said, not carried out. A visual argument for it would have to be honest about that.
Plate 5's last line states the second incompleteness theorem without an argument.
Plate 10 states Tarski's undefinability of truth as a known result; I have not worked it through on cardboard.
The tower now floats in the well of the wooden stair built round it; whether it reads from the landings, or is hidden by the rails, has to be judged standing there.

threads.why: The machine is a timed sculpture, not a search: its jam shows one attempt ending.
Finding can go on for ever while checking is finite, so a stopped search shows slow or broken, never impossible.
Without its three conditions the theorem certifies nothing: it is a mood.
Adding the sentence as an axiom works every time and is never finished.
Russell repaired once for good; here the totality exists and cannot be generated.
The theory cannot prove its own soundness; true-but-unprovable is said from one step outside.
Provable can be said inside arithmetic, true cannot: so the truth of the sentence is seen from outside.
Said with provable instead of true, the flipped row lands instead of contradicting.
A green light means something only after it has gone red: a limit on checking everything is not a licence to check nothing.
Add a critic and the blind spot moves; that is a reason to say what was checked, not to stop checking.
Fluent agreement is no substitute for the input, the rule and the result actually checked - including on this cardboard.
